      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Fallopian Tube <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Primary Peritoneal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> is a disease in which abnormal cells in the body grow out of control and form a <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span>. <span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is a cancerous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span> that forms in the tissues of an <span class="qt0">ovary. The ovaries</span> are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>There are a few different types of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The most common type is epithelial <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. It begins in the cells that cover the <span class="qt0">ovary</span>.</p><p>There are also two related types of epithelial <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that can spread to the <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>:</p><ul><li>Fallopian tube <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> forms in the tissue lining a fallopian tube. The fallopian tubes are a pair of long, slender tubes on each side of the uterus. The uterus is the female reproductive organ where a fetus grows during pregnancy.</li><li>Primary peritoneal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> forms in the tissue lining the peritoneum. Your peritoneum is a tissue lining that covers the organs in the abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>These two <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> are like <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, and they have the same treatments. So some medical experts also consider those two types as <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Some other rarer types of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> are malignant germ cell <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumors</span></span> and stromal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumors</span></span>.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes (mutations) in the genetic material  (DNA). Often, the exact cause of these genetic changes is unknown.</p><p>Most <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> are caused by genetic changes that happen during your lifetime. But sometimes these genetic changes are inherited, meaning that you are born with them. <span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that is caused by inherited genetic changes is called hereditary <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>There are also certain genetic changes that can raise your risk of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including changes called BRCA1 and BRCA2. These two changes also raise your risk of breast and other <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</p><p>Besides genetics, your lifestyle and the environment can affect your risk of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Certain people are more likely to develop <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. They include those who:</p><ul><li>Have a family history of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in a mother, aunt, grandmother, or sister</li><li>Have inherited changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes</li><li>Have certain other genetic conditions, such as Lynch syndrome</li><li>Have endometriosis</li><li>Took hormone therapy for menopause</li><li>Are overweight or have obesity</li><li>Are tall</li><li>Are older, especially those who have gone through menopause</li><li>Have never been pregnant</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may not cause early signs or symptoms. By the time you do have signs or symptoms, the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is often advanced.</p><p>The signs and symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, swelling, or a feeling of pressure in the abdomen (belly) or pelvis</li><li>Sudden or frequent urge to urinate (pee)</li><li>Trouble eating or feeling full</li><li>A lump in the pelvic area</li><li>Gastrointestinal problems, such as gas, bloating, or constipation</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam</li><li>Will likely do imaging tests</li><li>May do blood tests such as a CA-125 blood test</li></ul><p>Often the only way to know for sure that you have <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is by having a biopsy of the tissue. A biopsy is done during surgery to remove the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span>.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatments for <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery to remove as much of the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> as possible</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>Your provider may suggest that you have genetic testing to look for the gene changes that raise the risk for <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Knowing whether you have the gene change may help your provider decide on your treatment plan.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Paget's Disease of Breast</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer is a cancer</span></span> that starts in breast tissue.  It happens when cells in the breast change and grow out of control. New cells grow even when you don't need them, and old cells don't die when they should. These extra cells can form a mass called a <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span>.</p><p>Sometimes the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> does not spread any further. This is called "in situ." If the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> spreads outside the breast, the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is called "invasive." It may just spread to nearby tissues and lymph nodes. Or the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may metastasize (spread to other parts of the body) through the lymph system or the blood.</p><p>Breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is the second most common type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in women in the United States. Rarely, it can also affect men.</p>What are the types of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>There are different types of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The types are based on which breast cells turn into <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The types include:</p><ul><li>Ductal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">carcinoma</span></span>, which begins in the cells of the ducts. This is the most common type.</li><li>Lobular <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">carcinoma</span></span>, which begins in the lobules. It is more often found in both breasts than other types of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Inflammatory breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer, in which cancer</span></span> cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast. The breast becomes warm, red, and swollen. This is a rare type.</li><li>Paget's disease of the breast, which is a <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> involving the skin of the nipple. It usually also affects the darker skin around the nipple. It is also rare.</li></ul>What causes breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes in the genetic material (DNA). Often, the exact cause of these genetic changes is unknown.</p><p>But sometimes these genetic changes are inherited, meaning that you are born with them. Breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that is caused by inherited genetic changes is called hereditary breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>There are also certain genetic changes that can raise your risk of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including changes in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These two changes also raise your risk of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> and other <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</p><p>Besides genetics, your lifestyle and the environment can affect your risk of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is at risk for breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The factors that raise your risk of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Older age</li><li>History of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or benign (noncancer) breast disease</li><li>Inherited risk of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including having BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene changes</li><li>Dense breast tissue</li><li>A reproductive history that leads to more exposure to the estrogen hormone, including:
	<ul><li>Menstruating at an early age</li><li>Being at an older age when you first gave birth or never having given birth</li><li>Starting menopause at a later age</li></ul>
</li><li>Taking hormone therapy for meopause</li><li>Radiation therapy to the breast or chest</li><li>Obesity</li><li>Drinking alcohol</li></ul>What are the signs and symptoms of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The signs and symptoms of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include</p><ul><li>A new lump or thickening in or near the breast or in the armpit.</li><li>A change in the size or shape of the breast.</li><li>A dimple or puckering in the skin of the breast. It may look like the skin of an orange.</li><li>A nipple turned inward into the breast.</li><li>Nipple discharge other than breast milk. The discharge might happen suddenly, be bloody, or happen in only one breast.</li><li>Scaly, red, or swollen skin in the nipple area or the breast.</li><li>Pain in any area of the breast.</li></ul>How is breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to diagnose breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and figure out which type you have:</p><ul><li>A physical exam, including a clinical breast exam (CBE). This involves checking for any lumps or anything else that seems unusual with the breasts and armpits.</li><li>A medical history.</li><li>Imaging tests, such as a mammogram, an ultrasound, or an MRI.</li><li>Breast biopsy.</li><li>Blood chemistry tests, which measure different substances in the blood, including electrolytes, fats, proteins, glucose (sugar), and enzymes. Some of the specific blood chemistry tests include a basic metabolic panel (BMP), a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and an electrolyte panel.</li></ul><p>If these tests show that you have breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, you will have tests that study the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells. These tests help your provider decide which treatment would be best for you. The tests may include:</p><ul><li>Genetic tests for genetic changes such in the BRCA and TP53 genes.</li><li>HER2 test. HER2 is a protein involved with cell growth. It is on the outside of all breast cells. If your breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells have more HER2 than normal, they can grow more quickly and spread to other parts of the body.</li><li>An estrogen and progesterone receptor test. This test measures the amount of estrogen and progesterone (hormones) receptors in <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> tissue. If there are more receptors than normal, the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is called estrogen and/or progesterone receptor positive. This type of breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may grow more quickly.</li></ul><p>Another step is staging the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Staging involves doing tests to find out whether the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> has spread within the breast or to other parts of the body. The tests may include other diagnostic imaging tests and a sentinel lymph node biopsy. This biopsy is done to see whether the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> has spread to the lymph nodes.</p>What are the treatments for breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatments for breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Surgery such as 
	<ul><li>A mastectomy, which removes the whole breast</li><li>A lumpectomy to remove the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and some normal tissue around it, but not the breast itself</li></ul>
</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Hormone therapy, which blocks <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells from getting the hormones they need to grow</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li><li>Immunotherapy</li></ul>Can breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>You may be able to help prevent breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> by making healthy lifestyle changes such as:</p><ul><li>Staying at a healthy weight</li><li>Limiting alcohol use</li><li>Getting enough exercise</li><li>Limiting your exposure to estrogen by 
	<ul><li>Breastfeeding your babies if you can</li><li>Limiting hormone therapy</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk, your provider may suggest that you take certain medicines to lower the risk. Some women at very high risk may decide to get a mastectomy (of their healthy breasts) to prevent breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>It's also important to get regular mammograms. They may be able to identify breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in the early stages, when it is easier to treat.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ovariandisorders.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> Insufficiency</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>?<p>The <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones. Women have one <span class="qt0">ovary</span> on each side of the uterus (where a fetus grows during pregnancy). Each <span class="qt0">ovary</span> is about the size and shape of an almond.</p><p><span class="qt0">Ovaries</span> play a role in menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause.  Your <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>:</p><ul><li>Produce and store eggs that are released during ovulation (when an egg leaves the <span class="qt0">ovary</span> and travels into the fallopian tube). If a sperm fertilizes the egg, you can become pregnant.</li><li>Make the female hormones estrogen and progesterone.</li><li>Stop making those hormones and releasing eggs during menopause.</li></ul><p>Some medical problems can affect the <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>. These can cause various symptoms, and some <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorders may need prompt treatment.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorders?<p>Some problems that can happen with the <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> can include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is when a cancerous <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span> forms in the tissues of an <span class="qt0">ovary</span>.</li><li><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> cysts are fluid-filled sacs in or on an <span class="qt0">ovary</span>.</li><li>Polycystic <span class="qt0">ovary</span> syndrome (PCOS) is a set of symptoms related to an imbalance of hormones.</li><li>Primary <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> insufficiency is when your <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> stop working before age 40.</li><li><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> torsion is a twisting of the <span class="qt0">ovary</span>.</li><li>Endometriosis is when tissue like the lining in your uterus grows in other places in your body. It may affect the <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>, fallopian tubes, and tissue lining the pelvis.</li><li>Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection and inflammation of the uterus, <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>, and other female reproductive organs.</li><li><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumors</span></span>.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorders?<p><span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> disorders can happen for different reasons depending on the condition. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorders?<p>Your symptoms may be different, depending on the problem with your <span class="qt0">ovaries. Some ovarian</span> disorders, such as <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> cysts, may cause few or even no symptoms. Other disorders may cause more severe symptoms. Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Pelvic pain, which often happens during your period</li><li>Nausea or diarrhea</li><li>Vaginal bleeding that is between periods, very heavy, or longer than usual</li><li>Vaginal discharge</li><li>Painful menstrual cramps</li></ul>How are <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorders diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have a problem with your <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history</li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam</li><li>May order imaging tests, or blood tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorders?<p>Treatment depends on the <span class="qt0">ovarian</span> disorder, your symptoms, overall health, and plans for pregnancy. Treatment can include medicines, such as pain relievers or hormonal birth control, lifestyle changes to reduce symptoms, or sometimes surgery. <span class="qt0">Ovarian</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may require surgery, chemotherapy, or other targeted therapy.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hysterectomy.html">
      <content name="title">Hysterectomy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a hysterectomy?<p>A hysterectomy is surgery to remove the uterus (womb). The uterus is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. A hysterectomy treats problems like heavy bleeding, pain, or <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in the uterus.</p><p>After a hysterectomy, you no longer have menstrual periods and can't become pregnant. Sometimes the surgery also removes the <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> and fallopian tubes. If you have both <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> taken out,menopause symptoms will usually begin.</p>What conditions does a hysterectomy treat?<p>Hysterectomy is a major surgery. Your health care provider may suggest other treatment options first. These might include medicine, hormone therapy, or procedures to remove fibroids or stop heavy bleeding. Sometimes these won't help, or surgery might be the only option, depending on the condition that needs to be treated.</p><p>Your provider might recommend a hysterectomy if you have:</p><ul><li>Fibroids, if you are near or past menopause, have large fibroids or very heavy bleeding.</li><li>Endometriosis, that hasn't been cured by medicine or surgery.</li><li>Uterine prolapse, which can happen after several vaginal births, menopause, or because of obesity. It is when the uterus drops into the vagina.</li><li><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span>, of the uterus, cervix, <span class="qt0">ovaries</span>, or endometrium (the lining of the uterus).</li><li>Vaginal bleeding, that is heavy or unusual and persists despite treatment.</li><li>Chronic pelvic pain, which starts in the uterus. A hysterectomy is a last resort since it doesn't fix some pelvic pain.</li><li>Adenomyosis, is a thickening of the walls of the uterus. A hysterectomy is only considered if pain is severe and no other treatments have worked.</li></ul>What are the different types of hysterectomies?<p>Your provider will discuss the type of hysterectomy you need, depending on your condition.</p><p>The different types of surgeries include:</p><ul><li>A total hysterectomy is the most common type and involves the removal of all the uterus, including the cervix. The <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> and fallopian tubes may or may not be removed.</li><li>A partial (subtotal or supracervical) hysterectomy removes just the upper part of the uterus. The cervix is left in place, and your <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> may or may not be removed</li><li>A radical hysterectomy removes all the uterus, cervix, and tissue on both sides of the cervix and the upper part of the vagina. This is most often used to treat certain types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, such as cervical <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The fallopian tubes and <span class="qt0">ovaries</span> may or may not be removed.</li></ul>What methods are used for a hysterectomy?<p>A hysterectomy may be done several different ways. Your provider will determine the best method for the surgery based on your general health, the reason for the surgery, and other factors.</p><p>Methods to perform a hysterectomy include:</p><ul><li>Abdominal hysterectomy. A cut is made in your lower abdomen (belly). Your provider may recommend this method if you have a large uterus or to check other pelvic organs for signs of disease. This surgery has a longer recovery time than the others.</li><li>Vaginal hysterectomy. A small cut is made in your vagina. This may not be an option if you have very large fibroids.</li><li>Laparoscopic hysterectomy. Uses an instrument with a thin, lighted tube and an attached camera. This helps your provider see your pelvic organs. Small cuts are made in either your abdomen (belly) or vagina. This is not an option for all types of uterine fibroids.</li><li>Robotic surgery. Your provider guides a robotic arm to do the surgery through small cuts in your lower abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>After a hysterectomy, it can take four to six weeks to recover, depending on the type of surgery you have.</p>What are the risks of a hysterectomy?<p>Like all surgeries, a hysterectomy has risks, even though the results are usually good. Talk to your provider about the benefits and risks of having a hysterectomy.</p><p>More serious risks can include:</p><ul><li>Too much bleeding during surgery</li><li>Infection</li><li>Blood clots</li></ul><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Genetic counseling provides information and support to people who have, or may be at risk for, genetic disorders. A genetic counselor meets with you to discuss genetic risks. The counseling may be for yourself or a family member. Or you may get it when you are planning or expecting a baby. You may follow up with  genetic testing. </p><p>There are many reasons to seek genetic counseling. You may consider it if you :</p><ul><li>Have a personal or family history of a genetic condition or birth defect</li><li>Are pregnant or planning to be pregnant after age 35</li><li>Already have a child with a genetic disorder or birth defect</li><li>Have had two or more pregnancy losses or a baby who died</li><li>Have had ultrasound or screening tests that suggest a possible problem</li></ul></content>
